g.text: When the symbol-rate carrier-recovery story stops being enough

text.tspan: The π/4 alias note was always a 1-sample/symbol QPSK card.
This follow-up shows why the honest CFO window scales with observation rate,
and which front ends belong earlier once the symbol-rate view runs out of room.

g.text: 1. The alias limit scales with the sample rate seen by the estimator

text.tspan: For QPSK 4th-power coarse recovery, the honest window is |Δf| < F_s/8. If F_s = L R_s, that becomes |Δf|/R_s < L/8.

g.text: 2. The same physical CFO can alias at 1 sps and stay honest at 4 sps

text.tspan: This local toy check uses timed QPSK symbols, a hold-model oversampled waveform, and the same 4th-power
phase-difference estimator at 1, 2, and 4 samples per symbol.
At Δf / R_s = 0.30, the symbol-rate estimator folds to about 0.05 R_s, while the 4 sps version still returns the right coarse
answer. The dashed vertical markers show where each observation rate hits its own honest limit.

g.text: 3. Three honest branches once the symbol-rate view runs out of room

text.tspan: The point is not to inflate this repo into a full modem survey. It is to mark where the current symbol-rate packet ends
and which front ends belong earlier in the chain.

Minimal public reading: the old alias cliff note was never “carrier recovery in general.” It was a bounded symbol-rate
card. Once the CFO gets bigger, the receiver needs an earlier front end, not a louder claim about the same late-stage
